title: Gajendra lifts a lotus
hookLine: an elephant king fights a crocodile until his strength is gone, and Patanjali's one small word, or, opens a second road
carry: ishvara pranidhana: a road met from the other side
tomorrow: Death gives a boy one word. which one?

cards: Gajendra is the king of the elephants. In the Bhagavata Purana he wades into a lake on Mount Trikuta with his herd, and a crocodile clamps onto his leg. He pulls.
The crocodile pulls. His herd tries to help and can't. The fight goes on, the Purana says, for a thousand years, and the elephant, stronger on land, slowly loses to the crocodile in its own water.
His strength is gone. And then Gajendra stops pulling, and starts to pray.

teach.b: He doesn't call on a particular god by name. He prays to the one who is the source and shelter of everything.
The Bhagavata says that because the prayer named no single form, the other gods held back, and Vishnu himself came, riding Garuda.
Seeing him, Gajendra lifts a lotus in his trunk as an offering, and the crocodile is cut away. You sang this rescue in the arti on day one hundred twenty.
Patanjali has his own version of that turn. For twenty-two sutras he's talked like a coach: practice, let go, turn up the intensity. Then sutra 1.23: ishvara pranidhanad va.
Or, by devotion to Ishvara. Va, or: a second road. Ishvara means the Lord.

Pranidhana means setting yourself down before: devotion, surrender. The commentator Vyasa says that through this devotion the Lord turns toward the practitioner and favors them, and absorption comes near.
The road is met from the other side.
Like Gajendra, Patanjali names no particular god: sutras 1.24 to 1.26 call Ishvara a special seer, untouched by affliction and karma, all-knowing, the teacher of the most ancient teachers.
Scholars debate how central this is; many Hindu lineages take it as a real call to bhakti.
And that's the teaching: in Hindu devotion, surrender isn't giving up. Gajendra fought with everything he had, then let himself be helped.
Today it's the moment you've tried your hardest and quietly say, I can't carry this alone.

how: Many Hindu yoga lineages treat ishvara pranidhana as central, practiced through prayer, offering one's actions to God and repeating a divine name, while others teach it as one of several supports for meditation; many Vaishnavas also recite Gajendra's prayer from the Bhagavata.

o: a warning that one road is closed
va: the small word that opens a second road
a word that ends the list of practices

p: the elephant king held by the crocodile

s: Gajendra prayed before he had tried anything else
he fought for a thousand years, the Bhagavata says; the prayer came when his strength was spent.
Vyasa says the Lord favors the devoted practitioner
the Lord turns toward them and absorption becomes near.
Patanjali names Ishvara as one particular god
sutras 1.24–1.26 describe a special seer, all-knowing, the first teacher, with no single name or story.

games.q: Gajendra fought with all his strength, and it ran out. by the Bhagavata and sutra 1.23, what is the next step in Hindu devotion?
o: ishvara pranidhana: set yourself down before the Lord, and be met from the other side.
find a stronger technique and pull harder.
games.why: or, by devotion to Ishvara. Gajendra called, and Vishnu came; Vyasa says the Lord turns toward the devoted one.

practice: For the first part of this sit, try hard: return to the breath, alert, effortful.
Halfway through, set yourself down before God as you know God, perhaps with one quiet name, the way Gajendra lifted his lotus; if you don't pray, set yourself down before the stillness itself.
Let the effort soften, and notice what changes.

wordCard.voice: Or. The small word va in sutra 1.23 that opens a second road: ishvara pranidhana, devotion to the Lord, who meets the devoted one from the other side.

orig.note: Sanskrit īśvara: the Lord, the one who is able. in the Yoga Sutras, a special purusha, the first teacher.

carryVoice: Your line: ishvara pranidhana, a road met from the other side. Gajendra's lotus. Day four hundred thirty-six, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.2–8.3 (Gajendra and the crocodile; his prayer to the source of all; the gods hold back and Vishnu comes on Garuda; the lotus)
Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.23–1.26 (devotion to Ishvara; who Ishvara is)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.23 (the Lord favors the devoted one)
